title: Accommodating Machine Learning Algorithms in Professional Service Firms
pub: Organization Studies, vol. 45, no. 7, pp. 1009–1037 (2024); published online 23 May 2024
author: James R. Faulconbridge · Atif Sarwar · Martin Spring

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-level reconfiguration framing and adds comparative empirical evidence from early-adopting English law and accounting firms. It identifies uneven effects across professional tasks and shows extractive machine learning changing bounded document and diagnosis work more readily than relational or strategic work, while appropriately withholding conclusions about generative AI.
qs: This is also in line with the findings of Brynjolfsson and Mitchell (2017) who argue that analysis needs to focus on questions about the areas of work that machine learning technologies have the potential to reconfigure and how this relates to actual change.

For example, their analysis found that technologies ‘can be trained to help lawyers classify potentially relevant documents for a case but would have a much harder time interviewing potential witnesses or developing a winning legal strategy’ (Brynjolfsson & Mitchell, 2017, p.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, human-led deployment and materially extends it with empirical evidence about how firms reorganised work: automating bounded diagnostic tasks, assigning juniors verification and new responsibilities, reallocating technical work to technologists, and using partnership governance to legitimate change. Its pre-generative-AI scope limits generalisation but does not undermine the proposition.
qs: For instance, a lawyer described the need for junior professionals to now ‘quality check and sort of review what the [AI] tool has done’ (partner, law firm).

Partnerships not only allow professionals to block change as the existing literature suggests, but also allow professionals to retain a sense of control and to identify and legitimize acceptable changes to work when a decision is made to adopt machine learning algorithms.

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI-driven change is mediated by organisational choices, professional autonomy and occupational power rather than technical capability alone. Its accommodation framework shows professionals recursively shaping adoption and work organisation while responding to both machine learning’s contributions and limitations; it also leaves longer-term power shifts open rather than predicting a fixed technological endpoint.
qs: Accommodating machine learning algorithms involves strategic responses that both justify adoption in the context of the possibilities and new contributions of machine learning algorithms and respond to the algorithms’ limitations and opaque (Kellogg et al., 2020) and inscrutable (Anthony, Bechky, & Fayard, 2023) nature.

Accommodating machine learning algorithms is comprised of recursive processes enabled by the way professionals themselves control both how machine learning algorithms are incorporated into work and how work organization evolves in PSFs.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that machine learning changes legal production more than it replaces lawyers. Its interview evidence describes large gains in document-review speed and redistribution of routine work, while retaining human verification, legal judgment, transaction expertise and client relationships. It does not materially address pricing, buyer-side reallocation or provider-model restructuring.

kp.k: Evidence concerns early extractive AI adoption, not generative AI
kp.d: The authors studied accounting and law firms in England between 2018 and 2020, including 11 accounting firms and 19 law firms identified as early adopters. Most were medium-sized firms employing approximately 250–500 professionals, alongside larger firms. The document reports 876 documentary materials and 34 phase-one interviews followed by 52 phase-two interviews, although the introduction describes 80 interviews overall. Phase two focused on firms using similar extractive technologies, and the qualitative analysis developed a holistic explanation rather than comparing individual firms. Findings therefore concern this adoption context, before the subsequent expansion of generative AI.
qs: Between 2018 and 2020 we collected data by studying accounting and law firms in England.
This was based on insights from documentary materials (876 in total) and 34 interviews.
Phase 2 data collection involved 52 interviews to probe in more detail the adoption efforts
Extractive machine learning differs from generative forms of machine learning which generate new material, such as the written answers to questions that ChatGPT provides.

kp.k: AI automated diagnostic extraction while professionals retained advisory decisions
kp.d: Accounting tools such as Inflo and MindBridge identified potentially risky transactions; legal tools such as Kira and Luminance identified and extracted relevant clauses during document review. These supervised-learning systems made determinations about relevance rather than merely executing previously codified steps. Their outputs supported further professional review. The firms studied did not use emerging capabilities to recommend courses of action, which they considered nascent and too risky; inference, treatment and empathy remained relatively untouched.
qs: First, key tasks associated with diagnosis work (see Table 2 in the Appendix) were automated.
all of the packages used supervised learning.
All of the developers of the packages detailed in Table 3 emphasized the importance of the professional then deciding what to do with the data extracted.
none of the firms we studied used such abilities because, at the time of our study, such developments were nascent and perceived as coming with too many risks.

kp.k: Expanded review enabled new insights and client services
kp.d: Alongside automation, the authors found augmentation of diagnosis through reviewing entire transaction or document datasets and presenting patterns in visualizations and statistics. This enabled services beyond existing manual review practices. One law firm examined a client's force majeure clauses during Covid-19 to assess potential liabilities. An associate described emerging ambitions to predict claims, outcomes and compensation; these were reported possibilities, not independently demonstrated predictive performance.
qs: The visualizations of datasets and the production of statistics to represent the patterns found in the datasets were crucial as part of this augmentation.
Augmentation of diagnosis allowed professionals to offer new services to clients by redefining the purpose of diagnosis work.

We’re now starting to look at actually what does that data really mean, can we predict where claims are going to come from, what the outcomes are going to be, what the compensation values are going to be

kp.k: Cooperative adoption involved four reinforcing accommodation processes
kp.d: The central theoretical finding is that professionals accommodated machine learning through devaluing machine-learning-related tasks, legitimizing change, reinventing existing work and reallocating new work. The first two processes differentiated work suitable for algorithms from more valued professional work; the latter two reorganized tasks and occupational responsibilities. These were recursive, parallel processes with feedback effects, rather than a fixed implementation sequence.
qs: The latent codes were devaluing machine-learning related tasks; legitimizing change; reinventing; and reallocating.
Together, the two processes result in the differentiating of professional work
Third, accommodating machine learning algorithms is recursive with each contributing process operating in parallel and creating feedbacks.

kp.k: Devaluing junior diagnosis work reduced perceived professional threats
kp.d: Professionals regarded the diagnostic work affected by extractive AI as less valuable and meaningful than inference, treatment and empathy. Its concentration among juniors, who disliked it, limited disruption to the partners deciding on adoption. Participants justified change through better work quality, more meaningful advisory work and commercial benefits. The authors stress that some professionals mistakenly assumed, or chose to overlook, that extracting data itself involved algorithmic determinations and judgement.
qs: Hence, the completion of aspects of diagnosis work using machine learning was positioned as something that did not threaten the status of professionals and that could, therefore, be accepted.

the fact that this work was handled mainly by junior professionals, who disliked the work, reflected this and mitigated the impact on the more senior partners who were making decisions about the adoption of the technology.
any savings I can make there [with diagnosis] improve the profit I get out
AI is not taking away the complex tasks, the things where they have to exercise a judgement

kp.k: Junior work shifted toward verification and new analytical skills
kp.d: Junior lawyers and accountants adapted from manual diagnosis toward checking machine outputs and scrutinizing new visual and statistical representations. The authors describe time and training for continuous data review, real-time audit, project management and ongoing supervised training of algorithms. These findings establish changes in tasks and skill requirements, not quantified reductions in junior employment or changes in associate-to-partner leverage.
qs: reinventing meant junior professionals, who began to directly use the packages listed in Table 3, adapted to new types of work associated with diagnosis.
quality check and sort of review what the [AI] tool has done
what we call real time audit. So, we’re looking at live data
to supply the client with the business analysis or with the project management bit

kp.k: Technologists created new roles and internal career paths
kp.d: Firms reallocated installation, maintenance, integration and management of machine-learning systems to technologists, whose expertise combined technology with accounting or legal knowledge. These were non-fee-earning para-professional roles rather than replacements for the professional advisory role. The largest firm had 15 technologists; other firms typically had two to five. Titles included legal engineer, data scientist and innovation manager. Unlike conventional IT support, their decisions and participation in supervised training influenced professional work.
qs: A new role – the technologist – had been created and with it a new career path had emerged in firms, focused on the use of technology.
Crucially, in both scenarios, technologists were not fee earners within the firm.
The largest firm had 15 technologists at the time of our research
In other firms the numbers were lower – typically in the region of two to five individuals.

kp.k: Partnership governance enabled adoption through retained professional control
kp.d: Adoption decisions emerged slowly through dialogue, with partners retaining final authority. The authors argue that partnership governance and professional autonomy can enable cooperative change, not merely obstruct innovation: partners could approve changes that preserved valued work and block unacceptable ones. Technologists remained formally subordinate to professional priorities. However, the authors caution that professionals' sense of control did not fully capture technologists' substantive influence through expertise that professionals could not always understand.
qs: Partners, as senior professionals, need to be convinced of the merits of change, or technologies will not be adopted.
Similarly, reorganizing work has to be sanctioned by partners and can be halted if deemed inappropriate.
We thus reveal unbalanced power relations with professionals remaining in control, which enables cooperative adoption.
But it did lead professionals to feel reassured that they retained control over work (even if this reassurance was potentially misleading).

kp.k: Perceived risk mitigation did not eliminate algorithmic opacity
kp.d: Supervised training, trials and retaining human final decisions reassured professionals enough to permit adoption. Interviewees sometimes compared AI favourably with error-prone human reviewers, including a technologist's claim that models reaching 80%–90% accuracy would perform better. This was an interviewee's justification, not a measured study result. The authors conclude that such reassurance could rest on flawed perceptions: supervised training did not explain how subsequent determinations were produced or remove inscrutability.
qs: as soon as they’re 80%–90% accurate, they’re doing a much better job right?

This focus on the reassurance of supervised training misses the fact that the determinations being made after the period of training cannot be explained and unpicked, and hence the work done by machine learning remains opaque.
Intriguingly, however, our study also shows that the perception of risk being managed may be flawed, but still result in adoption.
Supervised training does little to overcome invisibility and inscrutability, given the lack of awareness of how the algorithms respond to the supervised training completed.

kp.k: Generative AI may unsettle the conditions enabling cooperation
kp.d: The authors explicitly leave open whether their accommodation mechanism extends to generative AI, which can affect more valued inference and treatment work. They ask whether professionals can devalue those tasks, whether partnerships will instead resist adoption, and whether technologists may eventually set the professional agenda. They cite Womack's 2023 report that 50% of England's top 50 law firms by revenue were not experimenting with or using generative AI as suggestive context, not evidence that resistance necessarily caused non-adoption. Future role reallocation and occupational power shifts are research questions rather than established outcomes.
qs: Generative machine learning algorithms are now capable of automating some tasks associated with inference and treatment work.
Hence, it is unclear whether the tasks they change can be devalued in the way that occurred when extractive machine learning changed diagnosis tasks.
50% of the top 50 law firms by revenue in England not experimenting with or using generative forms of AI (Womack, 2023).
Will they move on from being controlled by professionals and begin to set the agenda for professionals, using their knowledge of and ability to use machine learning algorithms?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Extractive machine learning automates parts of diagnostic work and augments professional analysis, while lawyers and accountants retain responsibility for advice and final decisions.
pts.d: Faulconbridge, Sarwar and Spring report that legal tools automate identifying and extracting relevant clauses for due diligence, discovery and contract review. Accounting tools automate identifying transactions requiring investigation. Reviewing larger datasets, potentially entire document collections or transaction populations, also generates new diagnostic insights through patterns, visualizations and statistics. The authors describe a law firm using force majeure clause analysis during Covid-19 to explore clients’ potential liabilities. These are findings about task automation combined with human-in-the-loop augmentation, not findings that whole professional roles or autonomous advisory services replaced lawyers or accountants. A mid-career law firm associate describes exploring prediction of claims, outcomes and compensation; this is an account of emerging use, not demonstrated predictive accuracy.

pts.k: Cooperative adoption depends on professionals distinguishing lower-valued work suitable for AI from valued professional work and retaining control over organizational change.
pts.d: The authors identify four interacting processes: devaluing machine-learning-related tasks, legitimizing change, reinventing professional work and reallocating new technical work. Professionals accepted changes when diagnostic tasks were regarded as less meaningful than inference, treatment and empathy, and when AI offered opportunities to improve services. Partnership governance enabled partners to negotiate, authorize or block changes rather than simply obstructing adoption. The authors also qualify apparent professional control: supervised training and retained final decision-making reassured users without necessarily resolving algorithmic opacity. Professionals could overlook the judgments already embedded in algorithmic extraction.

pts.k: AI changes junior professionals’ tasks and creates specialist technologist roles, rather than merely removing work.
pts.d: The authors report that junior lawyers and accountants increasingly check extracted material, scrutinize new analytical outputs, contribute to supervised training and develop project-management or continuous-data-review skills. Verification remains human work, including checks by more senior professionals. Firms allocate infrastructure, data and algorithm-management tasks to technologists, creating a distinct career path. These specialists combine technological and professional-domain knowledge and influence how AI is used, but in the studied firms they are non-fee-earners formally subject to partner control. The authors caution that partners’ sense of control may overstate their understanding of technologists’ decisions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central claims derive from qualitative research in early-adopting English accounting and law firms, supplemented by professional and media publications.
pts.d: The research covers 11 accounting firms and 19 law firms, including large international firms and the Big Four in accounting, but predominantly medium-sized firms employing approximately 250–500 professionals. The document review comprises 876 items: 587 Accounting Today articles, 271 Legal Week articles and 18 reports. Interview participants include partners, junior professionals, technologists and innovation or technology leaders. The article’s introduction states 80 interviews, whereas the methods table reports 34 in phase 1 and 52 in phase 2; this is an internal reporting discrepancy. The authors use manifest and latent coding to develop an integrated explanation of adoption, not a controlled productivity or accuracy evaluation. Accounts of speed, quality, profitability and predictive opportunities are participant experiences, expectations or vendor statements rather than independently measured general effects. For example, a law firm technologist’s 80%–90% accuracy statement is an adoption justification, not a study-wide benchmark. No quantified employment-displacement effect is established.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The observed findings concern supervised extractive systems used in 2018–2020; implications for generative AI remain conditional and explicitly unresolved.
pts.d: Although published in 2024, the study collected its empirical data between 2018 and 2020, before the widespread introduction of generative AI. The studied firms used extraction tools, not AI-generated client advice or automated recommendations about courses of action. Cooperative adoption was contingent on partnership autonomy, the particular technology’s capabilities, perceived benefits and risks, and changes concentrating on comparatively lower-valued diagnostic work. The authors state that generative systems can automate some inference and treatment tasks, but frame subsequent resistance, successful adoption, further task reinvention and shifts in technologist power as research questions rather than settled predictions. Their suggestion of longer-term organizational change has no specified deadline. They cite Womack’s 2023 report that half of England’s top 50 law firms by revenue were not experimenting with or using generative AI as suggestive evidence, not proof of why firms had not adopted it.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal effects fall on junior professionals, partners, technologists and business clients of established partnership firms.
pts.d: Junior lawyers and accountants bear much of the direct task change: less manual extraction or transaction screening and more verification and analytical review. Partners’ higher-valued advisory and relationship work remains comparatively protected, and partners control adoption and work allocation. Technologists acquire a new organizational role and career path, with specialist influence but subordinate formal authority; the largest studied firm employed 15 technologists, while other firms typically had two to five. Clients can receive broader diagnostic analysis and new risk-related services, illustrated by pandemic contract analysis. Some interviewees anticipate new markets, consultancy value and improved profits from diagnostic savings, but the study does not quantify those outcomes. Its evidence does not establish effects on access to justice, consumer legal markets, ALSP competition, profession-wide staffing ratios or net employment.
